summary: Defines a countersignature algorithm for CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE), along with the needed header parameters and CBOR tags. COSE provides security services for CBOR data. It updates RFC 9052. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A countersignature is when someone signs after seeing another signature, like a witness signing next to the author. This gives a way to do that for compact CBOR data.

questions: how to countersign a cose message
why was cose countersignature version 2 created
subtitle: A corrected way for a second party to sign off on any COSE message, not just signed ones.

tldr.problem: The countersignature algorithm in the original COSE specification (RFC 8152) did not always cover the cryptographically computed value, so its security properties were described incorrectly for some structures such as COSE_Sign1.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines version 2 countersignatures: a full form (COSE_Countersignature, header parameter 11) and an abbreviated form (COSE_Countersignature0, header parameter 12), both signed over a Countersign_structure that includes the extra values.
tldr.outcome: Implementers are encouraged to migrate from the old CounterSignature and CounterSignature0 to the V2 versions. The old labels (7 and 9) are marked deprecated, and the RFC updates RFC 9052.

today: RFC 9338 is an Internet Standard (STD 96) published in December 2022. It updates RFC 9052 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Countersignatures Were Redone
sections.content:
CBOR is a data format designed for small code size and small messages, and COSE defines security services for it, which suits constrained Internet of Things devices. A countersignature is a second signature that confirms the primary signature, much like a notary public witnessing that you signed a document.

While COSE was advancing to Internet Standard, it was noticed that the description of countersignature security properties for the COSE_Sign1 structure in RFC 8152 was incorrect. The COSE Working Group removed all countersignature text from RFC 9052 (which obsoletes RFC 8152), and this document defines a new countersignature with the desired properties.

The old algorithm did not always include the cryptographically computed value. The new one includes more values, except for COSE_Signature, which has no such value. For structures where that value was already included, the new algorithm yields the same countersignature value, so only the header parameter value has to change.
sections.plainLanguage: The first witness form had a hole: sometimes the witness did not sign the most important part. This RFC patches the hole.

sections.title: Countersignature Header Parameters
sections.content:
Two header parameters are defined. Countersignature version 2 has label 11 and holds one COSE_Countersignature or an array of one or more of them. Countersignature0 version 2 has label 12 and holds a COSE_Countersignature0.

The countersignature parameter can appear as an unprotected attribute in COSE_Sign1, COSE_Signature, COSE_Encrypt, COSE_recipient, COSE_Encrypt0, COSE_Mac and COSE_Mac0 structures from RFC 9052. Each parameter is optional in any given map.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the named slots on a message where the witness's signature is stored.

sections.title: Full and Abbreviated Countersignatures
sections.content:
A full countersignature uses COSE_Countersignature, which has the same structure as COSE_Signature. It can have protected and unprotected attributes, so the countersigner can identify its key and algorithm, need not be related to the producer of the signed object, and can itself be countersigned, a feature needed by protocols such as long-term archiving. Tagged, it uses CBOR tag 19. Only a signature algorithm with appendix may be used, because the body should be processable without evaluating the countersignature.

An abbreviated countersignature uses COSE_Countersignature0, defined as a bstr holding only the signature value. It supports encrypted group messaging, where the originator must be identified but the countersignature should be as small as possible. It has no protected attributes, so the key and algorithm come from the context used for the encryption, signature or MAC processing. It is encoded as an unprotected header parameter.

The two forms cannot be converted into each other, because the signature computation includes a parameter naming the structure used.

Countersigning means different things per target. On COSE_Signature or COSE_Sign1 it keeps the normal meaning. On COSE_Mac or COSE_Mac0 the payload is covered as well as the MAC. On COSE_Encrypt or COSE_Encrypt0 it attests only to the existence of the encrypted data, not the plaintext. To attest to the plaintext, sign the data first and then encrypt it.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a big witness form with room for notes about who the witness is, and a tiny one that is just the signature. You cannot copy one form onto the other, because the form's type is part of what gets signed.

sections.title: Signing and Verification
sections.content:
The signed bytes come from a Countersign_structure, a CBOR array with these fields in order: context, body_protected, an optional sign_protected, external_aad, payload and an optional other_fields. The context text string is CounterSignature, CounterSignature0, CounterSignatureV2 or CounterSignature0V2, depending on the structure and on whether other_fields is present. Fields are the target's protected attributes, the signer's protected attributes (omitted for abbreviated V2), application-supplied data, the payload, and an array of the target's byte string fields after the second. For a COSE_Sign1 that array holds the signature value.

To create a countersignature: build the structure, encode it to the ToBeSigned byte string, call the signature algorithm with the key, algorithm and ToBeSigned, and store the result in the signature field (full) or the Countersignature0 attribute (abbreviated). The target's own cryptographic functions MUST be finalized first. Verification mirrors this, and the application must also check that the key matches the signing identity and that the identity is authorized.

The narrowed deterministic CBOR encoding rules from RFC 9052 MUST be used so that all implementations produce the same ToBeSigned bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: To sign, you first write down everything the witness is vouching for in a fixed order, then sign that list. To check, you rebuild the same list and see if the signature matches.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Migration
sections.content:
IANA assigned CBOR tag 19 to COSE_Countersignature, described as a COSE standalone V2 countersignature. In the COSE Header Parameters registry it registered Countersignature version 2 (label 11) and Countersignature0 version 2 (label 12), and marked the old counter signature (7) and CounterSignature0 (9) as deprecated by RFC 9338.

Implementers are encouraged to migrate CounterSignature to CounterSignatureV2 and CounterSignature0 to CounterSignature0V2. New implementations must still support verifying CounterSignature (label 7) to stay compatible with senders following RFC 8152, while verifying CounterSignature0 may be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The old witness slots are crossed out on the official list and new numbered slots were added. Old messages can still be read, but new ones should use the new slots.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 9052 apply, especially the need to protect private key material. When COSE_Encrypt or COSE_Mac is used and more than two parties share the key, data origin authentication is not provided, since any key holder can compute a valid tag.

Countersignatures of COSE_Encrypt and COSE_Mac with short authentication tags do not give the security associated with the same algorithm in COSE_Sign. For 128-bit security against collision attacks, the tag length MUST be at least 256 bits. A countersignature of a COSE_Mac with AES-MAC (128-bit key or larger) provides at most 64 bits of integrity protection, and one of a COSE_Encrypt with AES-CCM-16-64-128 at most 32 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: A witness can only vouch as strongly as the thing they are looking at. If the original stamp is short and easy to fake, a witness signature on top does not fix that.
